name: Pedro Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining firms, AI companies, or political groups, and what you tell me stays confidential. What is a normal shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a haul truck and take the new operators through the safe route past the loading face. I check dispatch notes at handover, then spend most of the shift watching the road, the truck and the people on foot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which part of the work suits you, and what gets tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person the crew can rely on when a warning light comes up. The night rotation wears me down, and the pay is lower than I expected for the responsibility; I have less than a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quicker dispatch board would be handy if it did not hide why a route changed. I would still expect a trained operator to drive the truck and spot hazards the board cannot see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew to try the board if the mine shows us how it works. I would also say a few saved minutes do not make a low paycheck feel any bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My seat seems steady in this small-change picture, since most of my shift is hands-on. Still, thin savings and few nearby mines mean I cannot shrug off a missed week of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my rotation and use the dispatch board when it helps the handover. I would set aside overtime money for a month of bills before buying any new gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a little uneasy, not frightened about losing the truck in this version. The money cushion is still thin, so I would tell my partner Elena we should keep our weekend spending modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense would you trim first if overtime dried up, and who at the mine would you ask about shift cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pause the takeout meals first and ask my superintendent Mark whether another crew needs a relief operator. I would not borrow money for a tool unless it was part of paid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop using the dispatch board, and how would you check its advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it sent me toward a blocked haul road, I would stop and confirm with the radio operator. I would use the board after a few supervised runs, not because somebody said it was clever.

say: A dispatch board can help the **handover**.
Saved minutes do not fix my **low pay** or cover household bills.
think: Most of my shift is **hands-on**, so the truck seems steady.
Thin savings make a missed week **hard to absorb**.
do: Keep my **rotation** and use the board at every handover.
Set aside overtime for **one month of bills**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about money, but not frightened about this version of my job.
S0.quote: I would also say a few saved minutes do not make a low paycheck feel any bigger.
fieldNote: Pedro sees dispatch software as a **handover aid**, not a driver.
His **thin savings** create worry even in a mild scenario.
He wants **supervised proof** before trusting a new tool.

steps.text: Keep the current haul-truck rotation and use the board at handover
Set overtime aside until one month of bills is covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine could use AI to plan truck routes and write the maintenance notes before it tries robots in the pit. I would want the crew to see the system work on a normal shift before anyone changes the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we should learn the planning tools while they are still being tested. I would not say every operator is safe, because a mine can decide to run with fewer people even when trucks stay manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork and route planning in my lead duties might shrink first, and that could weaken my place on the crew. My driving skill is good, but there are not many other mines nearby if this one cuts positions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Mark to put me on a paid trial of the new route planner, then keep notes on where it gets things wrong. If the mine offers a maintenance certificate for operators, I would compare its cost and schedule before signing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the first change could reach my lead tasks even though robots come later. Elena and I have talked about a house deposit, and I would put that goal on hold if my hours started falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which sign would tell you the route planner is affecting jobs, and what would you ask Mark?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch whether open operator shifts stop being filled. Then I would ask Mark whether the trial changes headcount or just moves the planning work to a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the planner works well on another crew but makes mistakes on yours, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to run it beside the existing route sheet for a few shifts and report each mismatch. If the same error returned near the loading face, I would tell the crew to follow the safe route until it was fixed.

say: We should learn the **route planner** while it is tested.
Manual trucks do not guarantee the **same crew size**.
think: My lead planning duties could **shrink first**.
Few nearby mines make a **position cut** serious, with no easy transfer option.
do: Trial the route planner on **paid time** and record errors from each shift.
Compare the cost of a **maintenance certificate**.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lead work and a delayed house deposit.
S1.quote: I would not say every operator is safe, because a mine can decide to run with fewer people even when trucks stay manual.
fieldNote: Pedro sees **planning work** as an earlier risk than truck operation.
He would test software beside the **route sheet** before relying on it.
The **house deposit** is a concrete household goal that may be delayed.

steps.text: Trial the route planner beside the paper route sheet on paid shifts
Pause the house-deposit plan if operator hours begin falling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning side of the mine could change by 2028, and the truck side might follow with robots around 2031. I would have to make a choice quickly if the company started cutting shifts before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI arrives first and robots for hands-on work come about three years later. I would ask the mine to say which jobs it expects to keep, instead of telling us to stay positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose the lead part of my work quickly, and I do not have savings to wait out a long search. I am good at operating, but a certificate might be my best route into maintenance if a place opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask Mark for the mine's equipment timetable and apply for an operator-to-maintenance course if it is paid. In 2029, if the planning team had changed, I would take any open maintenance shift while keeping my truck qualification current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because this is a real threat to my hours, but I can still ask for training and look at internal openings. I would tell Elena we should not commit to a house deposit until we know what my roster will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no maintenance place opened in 2029, and which expense would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Mark whether a neighboring site needed a relief operator before I looked outside mining. We would pause the deposit and cut restaurant meals, but I would keep rent and family support current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether the course is worth taking before the AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a mechanic to show me the work and confirm that the certificate counts for an internal vacancy. I would not pay for a course that only gives me a paper without a chance to practice.

say: Thinking AI comes first; hands-on robots follow about **three years later**.
I would ask management for a **job-by-job plan**.
think: Lead work could change before I find **another post**.
A recognized certificate may open **maintenance work** at the mine.
do: Request the equipment timetable and a **paid course**.
In 2029, take an open **maintenance shift** if planning changes.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with training and internal openings still within reach.
S2.quote: I do not have savings to wait out a long search.
fieldNote: Pedro frames the risk as **lost hours**, not certain dismissal.
He has a **conditional maintenance plan** and keeps his truck qualification.
The couple would delay the **house deposit** rather than risk rent money.

steps.text: Apply for the mine's paid operator-to-maintenance course
Pause the house deposit until the roster is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to try a different skill while I am still employed. The thinking jobs at the mine change first, but robots do not reach the truck work until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the warning matters if the mine starts training people before it changes the roster. I would tell my friends that driving may last longer than dispatch planning, but nobody should count on that alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would rather move toward maintenance than wait for a robot to arrive at the pit. I have used the dispatch tools a little, so learning equipment records feels more reachable than changing to an office career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would spend the first year asking to shadow a maintenance crew one shift each month and check whether I enjoy the work. If it fits, I would finish the mine's certificate before 2031 and apply for an internal maintenance opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the money, but the five-year lead gives me room to test a path instead of jumping blind. I would keep my truck shifts until I had a confirmed place on a maintenance crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for during that first shadow shift, and who could tell you whether the certificate is useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch how the mechanics diagnose faults and ask what a new starter is allowed to do. Mark can confirm whether the mine recognizes the certificate, and I would ask for that answer in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, the first year after thinking AGI arrives, what would you do if your planning duties disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for an internal maintenance slot using the certificate and the service shifts I had shadowed. I would keep operating if the transfer took time, rather than leave before I had a written offer.

say: The warning matters if training starts **before roster changes**.
Driving may last longer than **dispatch planning**, but not forever.
think: I would rather build a route into **maintenance** than wait for robots.
Equipment records feel closer than an **office career**.
do: Shadow mechanics for one **shift each month** during the lead-up.
Finish the certificate and apply for **internal work**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but five years lets me test a path while employed.
S3.quote: I would rather move toward maintenance than wait for a robot to arrive at the pit.
fieldNote: Pedro chooses **maintenance** because it builds on his equipment knowledge.
Monthly shadow shifts let him test the work without leaving his **current job**.
He asks for a **written answer** on whether the credential counts.

steps.text: Shadow a maintenance crew for one shift each month
Finish the mine certificate before applying internally

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade is enough time for me to build experience in maintenance while I am still young. The planning systems would change around 2036, and the robots would reach the hands-on work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the extra time is useful if the mine lets operators learn on real equipment. I would tell Elena that we can delay the house deposit for a year while I see whether a certificate changes my options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when thinking AGI arrives, so I have time to change but cannot coast for a decade. I want a second skill that earns wages, not a hobby course that leaves me competing for the same few truck jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start the monthly maintenance shadow shift this year and save the overtime for the mine's certificate fees. In 2037, if the planning work had moved to AGI, I would apply for maintenance work and keep the truck license current until I had a new contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the long-run change but anxious about my money today. I can prepare over ten years, though I still need a stable roster to pay bills while I do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which proof would convince you that the mine's training is worth the time, and what if it is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see operators move into maintenance after the same course and find out what wage they received. If the mine offered no route, I would look at the neighboring site before spending my savings on private training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2037, if a maintenance job had not opened, what would you do next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Mark for a referral to another mine before the robots were due in 2039. I would keep the truck qualification current and postpone the house deposit until I had work lined up.

say: Extra time helps if operators learn on **real equipment**.
A year of delay may protect our **house deposit**.
think: At 37, I can change, but cannot **coast**.
I need a paid second skill, not **another truck applicant**.
do: Shadow the maintenance crew and save for **certificate fees**.
In 2037, apply for maintenance and keep my **truck license**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the future and anxious about money now.
S4.quote: I want a second skill that earns wages, not a hobby course that leaves me competing for the same few truck jobs.
fieldNote: Pedro uses the long lead to build a **wage-earning second skill**.
He needs evidence of **internal placements** before paying private fees.
A **nearby mine referral** is a fallback if his employer offers no route.

steps.text: Shadow maintenance staff for one shift each month
Hold overtime savings until the certificate route is clear

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I have little time to find a second role if planning jobs disappear. A paid maintenance course with real practice and clear internal vacancies would help more than a general promise to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A mining job is more than sitting in a truck; the handover, route and safety decisions matter too. I want the mine to count those skills when it decides who gets trained for the next role.

headlineQuote: A mining job is more than sitting in a truck; the handover, route and safety decisions matter too.
portrait: Pedro Usman is **27** and operates haul trucks at a large mine.
He is a highly skilled team lead with a technical diploma and **lower pay**.
He has **less than a month** of expenses saved and few similar jobs nearby.
He learns **new tools** after seeing them work on another crew.
He wants a **paid maintenance path** while keeping his truck qualification current.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to move from planning duties into another paid role.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid maintenance course**, practical shifts and clear internal vacancies would help Pedro make a planned move.
